title: Trump and Xi Can’t Stop the U.S.-China Spiral
gist: Orville Schell argues that neither Trump nor Xi is suited to the bargaining needed to stop the U.S.-China spiral: the May 2026 Beijing summit produced only a thin 'constructive strategic stability' amid ongoing supply-chain chokehold diplomacy, and the September 23 Washington summit risks backfiring if Trump feels spurned and reverts to retaliation such as new tariffs.

insights.claim: The May 2026 Trump-Xi summit in Beijing produced no breakthrough; it may have sustained a fragile peace Xi called 'constructive strategic stability' but did not change the fundamentally adversarial U.S.-China relationship.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Do not price durable detente from summitry; keep hedges on U.S.-China escalation.
insights.quote: But it did not change the fundamentally adversarial nature of the relationship between the two countries.
insights.locator: Sadly, no such breakthrough came to pass

insights.claim: The United States and China remain in a cycle of punitive 'chokehold' diplomacy in which each side exploits its control over critical supply chains to pressure the other.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Supply-chain weaponization (e.g., critical inputs, export controls) is structural; favor diversification beneficiaries and expect recurring shocks.
insights.quote: each exploiting its control over critical supply chains to pressure the other
insights.locator: Sadly, no such breakthrough came to pass

insights.claim: A second Trump-Xi summit set to begin in Washington on September 23, 2026 will face the same constraints as May's, so hopes for a conclusive breakthrough should be tempered.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Fade any rally on summit-breakthrough headlines; the base case is incremental management at best.
insights.quote: The same limitations that crimped the May summit will constrain the upcoming one.
insights.locator: Now, another Trump-Xi summit is scheduled

insights.claim: As long as Trump and Xi lead their countries, summits will at best barely manage the rivalry and at worst exacerbate it.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Personalist leadership on both sides caps the upside of diplomacy; U.S.-China risk premia should persist through both leaders' tenures.
insights.quote: As long as these two men lead their respective countries, the likelihood is that their summits will barely be able to manage the rivalry at best.
insights.locator: In the past, the United States and China achieved

insights.claim: Xi Jinping equates compromise with weakness and struggles with the reciprocal give-and-take at the heart of diplomacy, while Trump's pandering 'tech bro' side conflicts with his belligerent side, making effective bargaining almost impossible.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Expect deals, if any, to be narrow and transactional, and policy swings to follow Trump's mood rather than a coherent strategy.
insights.quote: Xi equates compromise with weakness and has a hard time understanding the give-a-little-to-get-a-little logic that is the heart and soul of diplomacy.
insights.locator: The problem is not simply that

insights.claim: Xi's statecraft draws on ancient Chinese legalism associated with Han Fei, which treats law as an instrument of state power and counsels rulers to stay aloof and hide their desires, making him impervious to personal flattery.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Personal-rapport diplomacy aimed at Xi is unlikely to shift Chinese positions; read Beijing through institutional interests, not summit optics.
insights.quote: When those who uphold the law are strong, the state is strong
insights.locator: American leaders love to personalize diplomacy

insights.claim: Xi, whose upbringing involved family hardship and betrayal and who has purged even friends, is more like Mao than any Chinese leader since and masks insecurity behind a facade of invincibility.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Opaque, control-focused leadership raises the risk of misread signals in a crisis.
insights.locator: Xi, in reality, is not a particularly secure man

insights.claim: Trump's China policy has swung wildly between conciliation and confrontation across his two terms, and little groundwork was done before the May summit to set expectations or convey a coherent agenda.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Policy volatility is itself the signal; tariff and export-control risk can re-emerge abruptly after conciliatory phases.

insights.claim: At the May 2026 summit, Trump was met on arrival by Vice President Han Zheng, only eighth in the party hierarchy, and there was no joint news conference or public university speech, while Trump's effusive praise went largely unreciprocated by an aloof Xi.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Beijing signaled it holds the stronger hand; U.S. leverage in bilateral talks is weaker than administration rhetoric suggests.
insights.locator: There were many other signs that Xi would not readily yield

insights.claim: Immediately after Trump left Beijing, Xi hosted Putin on his 25th visit to China in 26 years in power, signaling that China has other powerful partners and is less dependent on the United States.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: The China-Russia alignment is deepening; sanctions and trade pressure on either side is diluted by the other.
insights.quote: his 25th visit to China in 26 years in power
insights.locator: When I arrived at the Beijing airport

insights.claim: About two months after the May summit, Trump alleged unverified Chinese tampering in the 2020 election and announced new tariffs on China justified as discouraging forced labor.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Post-summit tariff escalation has precedent in 2026; don't assume summit goodwill protects China-exposed trades for long.
insights.locator: After all, it only took two months

insights.claim: If Trump feels spurned by Xi's impassivity at the next summit, he is likely to revert to retaliation, which could make the meeting even less productive than May's.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Watch post-summit rhetoric for signs of Trump feeling slighted as a leading indicator of new tariffs or sanctions on China.
insights.quote: Should Trump end up feeling so unrequited at this next meeting with Xi that he starts hurling more lightning bolts at China, this summit could end up being even less productive than the one in May.
insights.locator: After all, it only took two months

insights.claim: Past U.S.-China breakthroughs, from Nixon and Kissinger's 1972 opening with Mao and Zhou Enlai to Carter and Deng Xiaoping in 1979 and Clinton and Jiang Zemin in 1998, rested on genuine mutual respect, careful groundwork and trust-building, conditions largely absent today.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: A checklist for real breakthroughs: advance envoy work, mutual respect and public legitimization; absence of these means summits are theater.

insights.claim: The 1979 Carter-Deng summit accompanied the U.S. transfer of diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing, showing that past breakthroughs involved major concessions on core issues such as Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: Any genuine grand bargain today would likely require Taiwan-related concessions, a key tail risk for Taiwan-exposed assets.
insights.locator: When President Jimmy Carter and Deng met in 1979

insights.claim: Chinese leaders are steeped in fears that foreigners seek regime change in communist systems, so superficial flattery cannot substitute for the deeper confidence needed for deals.
insights.speaker: Orville Schell
insights.so_what: U.S. actions perceived as regime-threatening (human rights, election-interference claims) will harden Beijing's positions.
